utterances.text: Well, they discussed everything in general, the situation then, some of their errands, duties. In the morning they would comment on what had happened, on what -- if there had been any excesses, who had been brought in. On a couple of occasions I heard, "Squeeze should be put on him. He should be forced in some way." That was in the beginning when people were being -- still being taken for interrogation. So that was summer 1992 or -- specifically on one occasion, I heard it perfectly clearly when a driver, and I do not know which one exactly but he had some trouble with his car on the way between -- from Montenegro to Serbia, he had some trouble with the fuel, and then they said -- well, I cannot repeat their words, I cannot tell you who it was who said that, but they said, "It's those workers," that is we, the detainees in the mechanics shop; we were to blame for it. We sabotaged the thing and we should be punished for that. However, one of those drivers, and I'm not 100 per cent sure who that was, I think it was Drakul, he said, "No, nobody is to blame for it, and it's not those workers who are responsible for it. The problem was with the fuel filter, because that was clogged." Then once again -- I apologise, Your Honours. On another occasion I overheard, and I think it was the second or the third time, that the store room had been burgled and that was in the immediate vicinity of the restaurant that we talked about, and I heard their comments in the morning that somebody had burgled it during the night. And one of them said, "Well, there was nothing to steal from there because the Muslims had taken it all away." And I heard it perfectly clearly but then at that time there were no Muslims in the town so there was no way that a Muslim could have done that. And I heard then Mr. Mitar Rasevic say, "That's not true. It was not the Muslims. When we arrived in the KP Dom all the locks were all right. Only Serbs could have done it." And then the noise grew and then somebody said, "Well, perhaps, yes, some Serbs." I and a friend of mine, with whom I worked, he is FWS-210, afterwards, we went there, and again made a new padlock, had to weld, had to weld it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Rasevic and you recognised his voice. Did you recognise the voices of any other people participating -- not necessarily in that conversation but in other conversations from that room?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, very often one would hear Todovic's voice, the warden's voice, and all the other guards, because we knew them all. We knew all their voices. We knew them by their voices. We knew when it was Burilo speaking or Obrenovic. We heard them, and they talked about lots of things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that many of these discussions happened in the morning. Were there discussions about what happened the previous night?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, very often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we'll get to this point in a moment, but were there discussions about detainees being beaten? For instance, if they were beaten at night, were there discussions in the morning about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, now and then; not always. And I didn't always have an -- I couldn't always come close, because at times there were guards within the inside of the compound, so it was too risky to come close to the window, you know. But yes, there were conversations about that too, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these formal briefings in that room or were they more like social conversations where people are sitting around drinking coffee? Could you tell by the nature of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot really claim that it was official, because it was in passing and like that, even though some discussing about how to assign work and what duties, what errands. Yes, it did happen there, but I cannot really affirm that that was the only place, that that coffee shop was the place where they discussed and planned and held their business meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often did you hear the warden in that room, or in fact did you ever see him in that room when these discussions were taking place?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, we could not see anyone, because windows were painted white, so that we could only overhear them. And it wasn't always the warden and it wasn't always Rasevic and it was always Krnojelac -- I mean, Todovic. No. There were days when we wouldn't hear the warden's voice, when we wouldn't hear Rasevic's voice, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also mentioned the place -- the window in the workshop area where you were able to overhear. Were there any specific conversations that you overheard there that you recall?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: The metal shop, yes. Once I heard Relja, who was the foreman of the metal shop. He was absent that day. Now, his offices consisted of two rooms, actually, and they met there and drank and talked about all sorts of things. And on one occasion - I heard it very clearly - the discussion was general, about the situation, but in no time at all they moved on to talk about plunder. And I concluded from that discussion that they were talking about a place called Josanica, which is downstream from Foca, or rather, to the north. Some were saying -- one was saying about how he knew that his neighbours had all sorts of things, that we were very well off, but they didn't know that our houses were so full. And another one said, "We should have struck before this, but there was nothing to live on." Presumably they couldn't make their ends meet. And another one, the one who was -- who presumably always had information and he somehow stood out as a man who was in the know, a man who was well informed, he said, "Well, you know, my men, it wasn't all that easy, pick up a rifle and strike. One had to carry out all the preparations properly, and the preparations began when Tito died, because one had to do it in the police, in the media, in the politics. One had really to assign, select people, a proper cadre to create all the material reserves and then pick out the right moment to strike. And immediately after that my companions, my comrades who worked with me made a sign to me, and I just fled from the place. Which shows clearly that it was all planned and prepared, all that was then to happen. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zekovic, were you ever interrogated while you were at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us about the first time. When was it?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: The first time I was interrogated, about 25 days after my detention in the camp, and it was rather short. Inspector Koprivica was the one who interrogated me. He wanted me to describe to him in detail where I had been when the war started, whom I was seeing then, and about my movements at that time. And I told him all that. Of course, he knew all that. And he typed on a typewriter, this short record, which I signed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which part in the KP Dom did this interrogation take place?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Most people, including myself, were taken for interrogations to the second floor of the new wing of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the second floor, is that the floor that's the next one from the ground floor or is it the ground floor, first --

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the first one above the ground floor, so I would say that it's a two-storeyed building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When your interrogation was completed, what happened to you? Were you taken someplace?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was taken to the end of the hall where there is a staircase that leads to the ground floor. That's where Koprivica left me. He told me to wait, and he entered the first office where they were interrogating some people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anybody inside that room where somebody else was being interrogated? Did you hear what was being said?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: At the moment when inspector Vladicic walked out, as he opened the door, he turned his face again towards the inside of that room and he said, "Just hit him, do whatever, and he's going to admit whatever we ask him to." And then he turned around and saw me. He called out to a guard from the office and told him to take me to where I had been before that, and that guard took me to an isolation cell on the ground floor and locked me up in there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anybody else in that isolation cell?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that isolation cell I found three men, in terrible shape: beaten up. Two of them were lying on the floor and the third one was sitting with his back against the wall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us their names?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: One was Aziz Sahinovic. He worked at the Privredna Banka in Foca. And the other one was Rizvanovic. I don't know his first name, but his nickname was Ace. And this Aziz Sahinovic asked me to help him so that he could lean against the wall. He was in such terrible shape that he couldn't move by himself. Rizvanovic, nicknamed Ace, said to me quite literally, that's what I'm going to tell you, "Zeka, we are done in for tonight. Vukovic and Obrenovic are on duty and we are in deep trouble." That meant that there would be beatings again. And we could hear that almost every night in our rooms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for cross-reference, Aziz Sahinovic is mentioned in the indictment at paragraph 5.29. He's identified by the initials AS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you what had just happened to them, how they ended up in such bad shape in that isolation cell?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: They were beaten up, mistreated by the guards. They were there a few days before I was. We could not know exactly who was detained there and who was there for how long, but they were in terrible shape, I have to say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know how long they had been in that room by the time you arrived?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: They were a day before that for sure, but for how long even before that, that I don't know. Well, perhaps even a few days. They talked. Because not the same guards were there every night. And since they said that Vukovic and Obrenovic would be on duty that night, since they knew that, that could have well meant that they had been there for over two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the first names of Vukovic and Obrenovic, the two guards that they mentioned?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Obren Obrenovic, nicknamed Rambo. I don't know Vukovic's first name. I just know that he's from Cohodar Mahala and that he's tall and fair. I can't remember his name now, but on a list, I'd probably recognise his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, Obrenovic is listed on Exhibit P3 at number 46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Just so the court knows, the first name of the person listed at 46 is Dragomir Obrenovic, but we think that's the right person. Obren is his nickname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you in that isolation cell with those three men?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I didn't have a watch so I can't say. About an hour, an hour and a half, something like that, up to two hours. Not more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened at that time?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Then, again, the same guard who brought me there came. I don't know his name. He's one of the guards. And he took me upstairs to the first office where they were carrying out interrogations and he took me in. Inside, I found a young man from Cohodar Mahala, I can't remember his name exactly now, and they were finishing their interview with him. They said to him, "Well, see, you could have signed all of this, even without being beaten. It would have been better for you." Something like that. Koprivica said to this guard, "Why did you bring him? He's finished."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was he referring to as "him"?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Me. He said to this guard, "Why did you bring him? He has finished." And then he said, "Take him back to where he was." And then we went out of the office again. We went downstairs. He went towards the entrance office, a few steps away, to get the keys so that he could return me to the isolation cell, and at that moment, Inspector Vladicic came up and said, "No, you fool, not there. Take him back to the room." So, luckily, that time, I was not beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that there was a second time you were interrogated. When was that?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: That was after my attempted escape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get to that when we discuss that topic. Did you hear yet other people while they were being interrogated?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I worked in this administration building a few times in the new wing. I did some work on the locks. And I heard them shouting from one office. They were beating him. They were asking him to confess, to confess that he had made war reserves of water, because in his basement, they found a large barrel where he kept sauerkraut during the winter. In the spring, he put water into the barrel so that he could clean it, so that he could wash it, whereas they claimed that he was trying to stock up on water. And he said, "Why would I need stocks of water when I had water all round my house?" However, they were yelling at him and I heard them beating him and saying, "We know everything. You don't have to tell us anything. You don't have to lie. You don't have to justify yourself."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of that person who was being interrogated?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where he was from?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: From the outskirts of Foca, from Kamen up there. That's a village near Foca actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that person also detained in KP Dom at that time?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I didn't remember his name. He was with me in Room 18 when I was brought there. Later, when the workroom was set up, we were separated from the rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what eventually happened to that man?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Salko Mandzo ever tell you what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. When we met, when this workroom was set up, he told me what had happened to him. Before that, I saw when that had happened but I didn't know the details. However, when the workroom was set up, he told me that he had been interrogated, that they had tied his chairs back on the chair like this, that they beat him, that they mistreated him, and that at that moment, one of these men who were interrogating him, he didn't know what to say, whether they were policemen or whatever, that he put a knife by his eye and said that he would gouge his eyes out, and at that moment, the warden walked in and Savo Todovic, and then they said, "No, it's not that Mandzo. We need to interrogate a different Mandzo." Then they let him go. From the window of my room, I saw him walk into the yard. He was all faint. He could hardly walk. He was staggering, but they told him to go, but in that condition, he passed by the stairs and he started going towards that other area of the yard, and then the guards returned him from there too, and then he went to the gate again. And then at the gate, they said to him, "Why have you come again? Haven't you got enough by now? Go back to your room." He was all covered with blood, his face and his shirt. He wore a shirt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you actually able yourself to see Salko Mandzo walk back and forth in the yard all bloodied?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: I personally saw him. I personally saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any scar near his eye at a later date?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: I could not see the scar; I could only see that his face and shirt were bloodied. But I saw the scar later, later in our room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that Salko Mandzo told you that the warden and Todovic both came in. Did he say which of the two made the comment that it was the wrong Mandzo?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, he didn't say exactly. When they entered the room, they said that it was the wrong Mandzo, that they were supposed to interrogate another one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, Salko Mandzo is listed in Schedule B at number 36, and this incident is listed in the indictment at paragraph 5.28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zekovic, do you know what happened to Balic, Dzemo?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: When I was brought to the camp on the 20th of May, he was locked up in an isolation cell. Much later he was released. He was taken back to my room. He said that he was interrogated several times, that he was beaten, that he was mistreated. He could hardly move this hand. They forced him -- they were forcing him to sign some kind of statement that he had established some kind of units, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you how long he was in the solitary cell?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that he was in the solitary cell for over three weeks. I don't know exactly. I can't remember. But he was there for a long time, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zekovic, I'd like to ask you now about beatings that occurred in the evenings. Could you tell us whether there were beatings in the evenings and how they occurred?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Very often, practically from the very beginning, almost every evening; this would happen four or five, six evenings in a row, and then there would be an interruption for a day or two, so there were these irregular intervals. It was almost every evening. Sometimes it would last for an hour, sometimes it would last even longer. In passing -- I mean, this was all happening by the entrance, and sometimes it could happen in other places as well, but we could not locate those premises precisely. Usually it was people who were kept in this isolation cell were taken out for beatings, and often people were taken out of isolation cells that were within the prison compound. And often people's names were called out from rooms, and we could all hear and see that quite clearly, when they would come and call out people's name, and then soon after that you could hear horrible screams and moans and cries of these people. Later, when I started going out to the metal workshop to work, I could see the walls of this hallway, this entrance hallway, all bloodied. There were lots of bloodstains. And that's the way it was until the Red Cross came for the first time, when these walls were painted. Two inmates painted those walls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the entrance hallway located that you saw covered with blood?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: The entrance to the KP Dom. And then that's where people would pass, where prisoners would be searched, and that's where you entered the prison compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: To be absolutely sure, I'd like to have the usher show the witness Exhibit P6/1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you show us on this diagram where the walls were that you saw the bloodstains?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Here. The entrance into the KP Dom is here. This is where the entrance office is. This is where the gate to enter the KP Dom compound is. It's these walls, these walls, and these.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you slow down when you say "these walls"? Show us one wall, and then pause briefly and then show us another one.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm sorry. It's this wall here, opposite the door; this wall by the door; and the wall on the side facing the interior part of the camp. Here, in the corner, there was a metal wardrobe for clothes, and there were bloodstains on that too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Let the record reflect that the witness has indicated a wall to the left as you walk into the entrance to the KP Dom, the wall directly in front and also the wall to the right. When he described the metal wardrobe, he was indicating the corner to the left and front, so that if you're coming through the metal gate in the inside of the courtyard, it is directly in front of you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to see where people -- well, first of all, you said they would come and call out names from the rooms. Who are you referring to as "they"? Who would come?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: The guards. That was always in the evening. Those who were on duty that evening, their shift would start at 7.00 and it would always happen after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how the people were chosen to be taken out?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: It would be hard for me to give you an accurate answer, precise answer. Some people were taken out several times; others were taken out that way and they were never returned to the room, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able personally to see where people were taken to?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean, could I personally see where they were taken to? When they would take them out of the room, they would open this metal door, and that same second you could hear screams and moans, and sometimes it would go on for an hour, sometimes even longer than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is the same metal door that you described as where you would have to wait when you were being taken out to work; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's that metal door. I'll never forget that sound until the earth covers my eyes in my grave. Because we would hear that sound and we would be startled, because we knew that nothing good would come out of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What other sounds were you able to hear? Were you able to hear people's voices?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: We heard those people screaming, crying, begging, saying that they're not guilty of anything, that they don't know anything. Once I heard, quite clearly, they asked a man -- I mean, I didn't hear the man being asked where his sons were, but I just heard the man say, "I don't know where my children are. I don't know where my children are," and they beat him mercilessly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the people involved in the beatings? Do you know if they were military, for instance, or if they were guards? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Guards came to the rooms and they took men out. And now, at the gate, whether there was someone else there, someone who came from the outside, that we couldn't see and that we couldn't know. However, it would happen that soldiers came there too, and members of this so-called military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say soldiers came there, did you actually see soldiers at that metal gate?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see soldiers during the day and in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when people were taken out to be beaten, you also saw soldiers?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Could not see then. Then I could only see and hear the guards coming and taking people out. Who was down there, that we could not see. By this entrance door, I can show it to you in the picture, there was a window, but thin wooden boards were put there instead of glass so you couldn't see through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that what you called the so-called military police were involved?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: I know. One evening I heard with perfect clarity their commander, that's what he called himself, Coso, they took five or six men from the rooms, they beat them down there, and at one moment, I heard Coso's voice clearly when he said, Nurko, do you know what happened to my Bota?" And he said, "How should I know?" They were beating those men for a very long time. And then I heard his voice, I heard him say, "Well, you can stop now." That lasted for a long time. We knew by the sound of the car that would come in front of the KP Dom, which car it was. They came in a yellow Volkswagen which had a characteristic sound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said, "I heard him say, 'Well, you can stop now,'" whose voice did you hear say that?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Coso's. That's this commander of this military police, Cosovic, Coso.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you able to recognise his voice? Did you know him from before?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him from before, for a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what capacity did you know him?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: I knew him by sight. We would see each other in town and also on rafts on the Tara. We were not friends but I knew him perfectly well. Also, it would happen that we would be in the same cafes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know other members of the military police?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: I knew most of them by sight. Most of them I knew by sight. But I wasn't friends with them before the war. And almost all the members of that so-called military police were known from before to prosecution authorities in Yugoslavia and abroad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a comment that you said Coso's made about Bota. Who was Bota, do you know?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a member of his so-called military police. That day, they set off on a mission in the area of Tjentiste and somewhere ran into a mine with a vehicle and that Bota was wounded in the spine, and then they came down to the KP Dom to take revenge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you learn that, what happened to Bota at Tjentiste?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard him ask then, "Do you know what happened to my Bota?" So I realised that something had happened to him but, and later on I heard that he had been wounded. Because later on, when I was in the metal shop working, some members of that so-called military police would come, and one of them was Coso, and another one called Djura and some others, and from their conversations, we just learned what had happened. You should know that we had a specific manner of collection of information, and that is you just strain your ears to eavesdrop as much as you can, to overhear as much as you can, whenever you pass by other people, whenever communicating with people around us, and from those odds and ends of information, we tried to put that together and thus came by rather reliable information. About this particular incident, I know specifically because I heard about it from those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those military police? Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a yellow Volkswagen. When did you hear the sound of that car? Before or after the beating?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Before and after. First, when they would arrive to the camp, and then after, afterwards, when they left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the beating of -- that you described, where Coso made the comment about Bota, after the beating, did you hear anything else? You talked about the car but did you hear any gunshots?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes, yes, we heard gunshots, I and many other people in the camp, in rooms. Though many people -- those were horrible moments and some people fled to upper bedrooms and would cover their heads with blankets not to hear those screams, those painful cries of those poor things. And I, yes, I heard shots, shots from a revolver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described other people covering their ears. Did you do that or did you listen?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't cover my ears. I had -- I don't know how to put that but I -- somehow, I had the courage. I wanted -- I wanted to hear as much as possible, to learn, see as much as possible, so that if I survived, I could tell others what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described gunshots. Could you tell us how many you heard?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly whether five or seven, but because, of course, there is an echo there but not less than five, maybe six.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened --

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I'm not being precise. Five, six or seven. But it did happen, except that I cannot really affirm if it was six or seven or five. I suppose if you collect more information, you will find out how many people were killed then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While this was happening, do you know if anybody was in the warden's office?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Lights were on. Yes, there were lights on, and we could hear people come in, go out, even though it was in a different wing of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you hear after the gunshots?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: After those gunshots, we heard a car engine being switched on in front of the KP Dom, in front of the camp, and by the sound, we identified that car, we knew that it was from the metal shop, that is a Zastava car, that is something like a pickup vehicle. People who were in Room 13, I spoke with them later on, it was that gentleman whom we mentioned FWS-210 and another one who worked with me in the metal shop, and he -- I think he must have been killed because I don't know where he is. Nobody knows where he is. Uzeir Hadzalic, they told me how they could see the stairs, the staircase, how those bodies wrapped in blankets were taken down and out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell by listening where the Zastava car went?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: The distance was very -- the distance covered was very short, 100, 150 metres perhaps, and then the engine was switched off. That is what I could hear, I couldn't hear anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The following morning, did you actually see that Zastava car, that pickup truck?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The next morning I saw that car in the metal shop area. The next morning, we were not taken to work outside so that only this friend of mine whom I just mentioned, number 210 and I were the only ones who went into the metal shop area, into its yard, to pick up some letters that we had made for Room 13, and the boring machine and the welding device and other tools that we needed, and in the metal shop yard, we found that car. It had been just washed. I mean five or ten minutes before that. So that water was still dripping. And in the grooves where the rear part of the car, the freight part of the car, one could clearly see traces of blood.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'd like to have the witness shown Prosecution Exhibit 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you point out to us where this metal shop was and where you saw the car, approximately?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the metal shop yard and the car was here in front of the locksmith's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the car usually kept there?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, not in a strictly defined area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the entrance to the metal shop area, could you show us if there was a gate?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a metal gate, a wide gate for large trucks and a small one for the staff, and it is this one here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that gate which you're indicating as being to the left of the entrance into the KP Dom compound, was that gate normally locked?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: That gate was always closed and locked, and one entered into the metal shop on the left-hand side, left of the entrance into the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you. And just for the record, Your Honours, the place where the witness was showing the car's location was inside what we could call the courtyard of the metal -- of the workshop area, and that would be to the left of the gate, which is to the left of the entrance into the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: When you say "to the left," you mean from the inside?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I mean as we are looking at Exhibit P6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, on the exhibit. Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did the car belong to? Was it a KP Dom vehicle?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was it used for?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to carry certain things, for deliveries, for smaller-size production materials, or for the KP Dom as a whole, for the metal shop, the production materials for the metal shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a specific driver of that car?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not a special one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it always KP Dom staff who drove the car?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, always. Somebody -- yes, somebody from the KP Dom, sometimes a driver and at times a guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you recognised that car by the sound. What was specific about the sound?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's true. The exhaust pipe was faulted, and we knew already about that from before, so it had a very characteristic sound when it worked. It was very loud.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in relation to the yellow Volkswagen that you described, were those sounds different?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. But of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To whom did the yellow Volkswagen belong?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: The military police, but they had very many vehicles, because they simply picked them up around the town, any number they needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you repair those cars, and that's how you're familiar with them?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for instance, not this yellow Volkswagen, but vehicles which were in the KP Dom compound, yes, we did. And once we had to repair the car for the commander of the so-called military police. He found the car somewhere, that is, simply robbed somebody of his jeep, and the car was in the car shop. But we from this metal shop had to make the roof; that is, we made tubes, iron tubes, and we had to mount them so as to cover, to cover the roof for the canvas. And Cosa came to the -- downstairs to the -- down to the KP Dom on various occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what access the military police or, indeed, other members of the military had to the KP Dom at this time?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose free, free, free access. I mean, I don't know. Once, a neighbour of mine, Dragan Zelja, he came in the evening - it was already past 8.00 - brought me a package of cigarettes, which means that he could enter freely. And likewise, those others who came to the metal shop, whenever they needed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your neighbour, Dragan Zelja, what is his last name? What is his family name?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Zelenovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What function did he have in the military?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: How could I know that? He did not tell me. He did not tell me whether he had a rank or an office or something. I know he was a member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a member of the military police?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if he was present when Nurko Nisic was being beaten? Did you --

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose and I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you suppose so?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Because he was a part of this narrow circle, Cosa's circle, and I'm -- yes, I'm quite confident that he was there, and he was also great friends with that Bota.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear Zelja's voice that night when Nurko Nisic was being beaten?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say 100 per cent, but I think I did, yes. He speaks very fast. That is his characteristic. Although it was difficult to tell one from the other precisely, but I think he was; I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the night that you described when you heard the gunshots, could you tell us who was taken out, who was beaten?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Nurko Nisic, Mustafa Kuloglija, I think, and I can't remember the names now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Nurko Nisic, Your Honours, is C-19, and Mustafa Kuloglija is C-15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see either of those two men again?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to move on now and ask you about some exchanges, or people being taken out for so-called exchanges. Can you tell us when those things happened?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: People were taken out for exchange on various occasions in the summer of 1992, in August and September. There were exchanges about which we knew had been carried through, that is, that people had been set free, but many of these exchanges never went through. I saw with my own eyes several times from the metal shop compound groups of people being taken out with their hands tied at their backs and beaten from all sides, and there were both military and KP Dom -- or rather, camp personnel. They drove those people away and they were never seen alive again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you able to see over the gate of the metal workshop?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, naturally, from the ground. If you were close to the gate, you could not see it, but if you moved further away from the gate, because the yard of the metal shop, there is some elevation, there is a slope, so you could see then. But in the metal shop area, at that time, we always had a metal kiosk made of metal tubing, some two and a half to three and a half or four metres. I'm not quite sure how large it was. And as we were to work at a height, we had a kind of a scaffolding and we would climb that. So I would climb that and I could see clearly what went on in front of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I'd like to have the witness shown Exhibit P6 again and ask you to show us the area that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have said this is the metal shop gate, this is the entrance into the camp building, here, in front, in the front part of the metal shop, that is, the locksmith shop, in the area, in the yard. So in front, outside, in the open air, was this kiosk which was being built all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you show us where you saw the detainees being led out?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Here. Here, at the gate, the main entrance, in front. And the car was turned -- well, a couple of times it was a kind of a van, and once it was an army vehicle, a freight vehicle. And I saw this from here, over the fence. It was about 25, 30 metres away, perhaps a metre or so more, but one could see it clearly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you see, as the detainees were led out, if the people beating them used any weapons?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They had those standard police truncheons and the pieces of very thick cable. I mean electric cable, very thick one. And many also had automatic rifles and carried them, and they beat with those parts, with butts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did you see this type of incident?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw it three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to recognise some of the detainees who were taken out in this way?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: In a group, in one of the groups, I recognised, although there were quite a number of guards around them and those troops, but I recognised Ramo Dzendusic, Mersud Pasovic and Kemo Isanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any of those three men again?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear any discussions among the guards or soldiers about exchanges? Or did you actually ever have any conversations with them?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: We received some information from some guards too, and sometimes information from people we could meet around the KP Dom, around the camp, and outside -- outside the KP Dom compound when we went to work, out in the field, to put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody ever tell you what happened to the people who were taken out? Were they exchanged?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Once, in the yard of the compound, I came across a soldier who used to work at the same place where I did before the war, and we knew each other well, and he told me, "Well, a couple of days ago, I escorted -- I was an escort and your uncle was exchanged at Rogoj." So those men were set free. But about a number of those exchanges, that is people who had been taken away, but -- well, and we never heard from them so it was sort of -- well, it's logical then that they must have been killed, but nobody said that. But somehow we did not know and we do not know. But there were guards, there were guards who told us, who told me, and this person who is indicated here, 210, "If they call you for exchange, to refuse it, to say, 'We don't want to go. We don't want to be exchanged. We don't want to -- we don't want to be sent to fight.'" So they must have been abreast of what was going on. And I and this friend of mine, who is mentioned here, we once wrote a kind of an application, a kind of request that we handed to Savo Todovic, asking not to be exchanged. And there was yet another thing which was very characteristic. In the summer of 1992, the end of the summer, late summer, a group of workers was taken away, that is of skilled workers, those who worked with us in the metal shop, were taken away, Suad Islambasic, Abdulah Kameric, Uzeir Hadzalic, who else? Can't now, the names escape me now. But they were taken for an exchange, and when Relja returned the next day -- he was absent at that time. The next day, he walked around, he seemed to be out of his mind, he was walking up and down the yard, "They've taken away skilled workers, good workers. Who will work from now? They are asking me to finish the work, to complete this and complete that, and they took my best workers away." And after that, a list was compiled, even though, of course, it was clear who had stayed behind. Savo Todovic made a list of us who worked, and nobody else was taken for exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Relja ever tell you who made these lists for exchange?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you who made work lists?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC
utterances.text: Those lists were made by the warden and by Savo. Because once I -- I asked. He said, "Well, Zuti, Lija, are going to the hospital," and yet another one from Jelec, I can't remember his name. And I said, "Relja, why don't I go?" Because I knew quite a lot of people down there because my wife used to work in the hospital. And he said, "I can't do anything about it, Zeka. What the warden and Savo write down, those they assign have to go. I can't do anything about that." And then I said, "Well, I'm -- I know those things better. Zuti and his brother are not really particularly qualified to do that. I know better how to do the job." But it was of no avail.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We will resume at 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
